1.pericope_label: Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees... Without me they shall bow down under the prisoners, and they shall fall under the slain

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the chapter division misleading: these four verses continue the preceding discourse and end with its tolling refrain, while a new section begins at the fifth verse and runs for two chapters, the first in the collection dealing exclusively with Assyria. He hears a touch of irony in the questions, asking whether those corrupt judges had considered what they would do when the Supreme Judge called them to account, whether they had an ally or a hiding-place for the treasures they had made their glory; and he reads the closing verse, obscure as it is, as the answer to those taunts, the prophet dropping the direct address for an ominous aside in which there is no ally and no hiding-place, only bowing among the captives or falling among the slain. Delitzsch reports that poor men who wanted to begin proceedings were not even allowed to and that property to which widows and orphans had a well-founded claim was welcome booty, and notes that the word for visitation always means a visitation of punishment while the word for desolation is a dull confused rumbling, said to come from afar because a distant nation was the instrument.

Gill raises the smaller doubt whether the opening word is a threat denounced, as the ancient versions took it, or a vocative summons, as the Jewish grammarians read it; he describes laws that discouraged the poor from applying for justice and vexatious suits that wore them out when they did, the cause going generally for the rich; and on the closing verse he lists the options without choosing, that they are forsaken by God, or bow because they are not his people, or, on a rabbinic reading, that the word means besides, so that beyond the subjection suffered at home a greater affliction is coming in captivity. Calvin says the poor were robbed for the rich and went away mocked from the judgment-seat, singles out the destitute because they lack help while magistrates who owe them more assistance take greater liberty in oppressing them, and turns on the princes as careless and indolent in their distresses, men intoxicated by prosperity who despise danger; though God delays, he insists, the time is fixed and near. On the last verse he gives two readings without preferring either, the exclusive sense that all will be given up to captivity or death, and the causal sense that their ruin comes of revolting from God, which makes the words an ironical reproof of the ungodly, who boast of being forsaken as though nothing were more desirable than to withdraw as far from God as possible.

Clarke renders the difficult particle of the fourth verse without my aid, so that they are taken captive by the captives and subdued by the vanquished, and draws the moral that as they had lived without God in worship and obedience they should now be without his help. Wesley identifies the far country as Assyria, accounts for the security of a people in amity with the Assyrians next door, and says the same as Clarke of the closing verse more briefly, that they are without the favour and help they had forfeited.

Henry leaves open whether the princes of Israel or of Judah are meant but draws out what hangs on it: if Israel's, these verses join the previous chapter, which the repeated refrain makes probable; if Judah's, they show why God brought the Assyrian army, to punish magistrates for a maladministration no one could call them to account for by law.

debates.question: Whose rulers are under this woe?

positions.view: Undecided, but the answer determines whether the passage continues the previous chapter or explains the Assyrian invasion of Judah.
Israel including Judah; the four verses belong with the preceding discourse, and the new section starts at the fifth verse.

debates.question: What does the difficult particle in the closing verse mean?

positions.view: Without my aid: they are captured by the captives and subdued by the vanquished.
Either forsaken by God, or not his people, or the word means besides, a further affliction beyond the present one.
Either exclusively, that all are given up to captivity or death, or causally, that their ruin comes of revolting from God.
The text is obscure, but the clause answers the taunting questions: no ally, no hiding-place, only exile or death.

outliers.note: Turns the second reading of the closing verse into an ironical reproof of the ungodly, who boast of being forsaken by God as though nothing were more desirable than distance from him.

themes: Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed;
To turn aside the needy from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey, and that they may rob the fatherless!
And what will ye do in the day of visitation, and in the desolation which shall come from far? to whom will ye flee for help? and where will ye leave your glory?
Without me they shall bow down under the prisoners, and they shall fall under the slain. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.

5.pericope_label: O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the same division of the book as Clarke, noting that Assyria had been mentioned before but that this is the first utterance of which it is the direct subject, so one might call it the burden of Assyria. He then supplies the history from the monuments: Damascus taken and Samaria reduced, two kings doing homage to their common overlord at Damascus, a new king beginning the conquest of Samaria and carrying off the ten tribes, and on his death the throne seized by his own commander-in-chief, who says in the Khorsabad inscription that he besieged, took and occupied Samaria, carried into captivity twenty-seven thousand two hundred and eighty of its inhabitants and set his own lieutenants over it, and in a damaged inscription calls himself conqueror of the far-off land of Judah. It was probably to this king, Ellicott concludes, that the words are addressed, and not to the successor commonly supposed before the inscriptions were read.

Gill lists three readings of the opening word: a call summoning the Assyrian against the land, a sigh that God must use such an instrument against his own people, or a threat of ruin, since the ancient versions render it woe, in which case the verse begins the comfort rather than the sentence. He adds that the Assyrian is called the rod of God's anger because he was used as an instrument to chastise Israel for their sins. Calvin works through the same range and changes his mind in the open: the particle is sometimes lamentation, sometimes address, sometimes a woe, and his first thought is that God assumes the character of one who sighs at having to punish his people so, but on closer examination he prefers the summons, God arming the Assyrians with his authority as a judge calls an officer to chain a malefactor.

Clarke calls this a new and distinct prophecy running to the end of the twelfth chapter, and dates it between Hezekiah's sixth year, when Samaria fell, and his fourteenth, since it foretells the invasion that came then. On the text he judges that the word standing for the staff itself embarrasses the sentence, and omits it on the authority of the Alexandrian Greek and ten manuscripts, reading his staff instead; an archbishop, he reports, was likewise dissatisfied and proposed a different remedy, changing one word so that the clause runs that he is a staff in the day of mine indignation. Wesley takes the opening as an invitation to the Assyrian to take the charge and set about the work, and says God's anger against his people is what puts the weapons of war into Assyrian hands.

Henry keeps the older identification of the king and frames both halves of the story, the destruction of the northern kingdom foretold in the preceding chapter and accomplished in Hezekiah's sixth year, and the correction of Judah foretold here and falling in his fourteenth, when a later Assyrian king took the fenced cities and besieged Jerusalem; the point he draws is that God deputed that king his servant and used him as a mere tool. He alone turns the verse back on the people, a hypocritical nation professing religion and at that moment reformation, but not so good as they pretended now that a pious king had brought goodness into fashion.

debates.question: What does the word opening the verse do?

positions.view: Any of three things: a summons, a sigh of grief, or a woe threatening ruin.
A summons, on reflection, though a sigh was the first thought: God arms the Assyrians with his authority as a judge calls an officer.
An invitation to take up the charge and begin the work.
The king of the great invasion, on the older identification.
His predecessor, the usurper of the inscriptions, and not the successor commonly supposed before they were read.

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse back on the people it comforts, calling them a hypocritical nation not so good as they pretended once a pious king had brought goodness into fashion.
Deletes a word from the received text on manuscript authority and reports an archbishop's rival emendation of the same clause.

themes: O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation.

6.pericope_label: I will send him against an hypocritical nation... Shall I not, as I have done unto Samaria and her idols, so do to Jerusalem and her idols?

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the verb will bear I will send, I did send, or I am wont to send, and prefers the last, making the commission not a fact in history nor an isolated prediction but a law of the divine government; he would render the nation impious rather than hypocritical, and hears in the words for spoil and treading down a memory of Samaria's fall. The thoughts the prophet puts into the Assyrian's mouth match the egotism of the inscriptions, where I conquered, I besieged, I burnt, I killed, I destroyed is the recurring burden; behind the boast about the princes he sets an Assyrian king's list of twenty-three who came to do homage at Damascus; and he observes that idols is hardly a term of scorn in an idolater's mouth, supposing the prophet put into his lips the word he would himself have used. Delitzsch puts the hinge compactly: Asshur was to be an instrument of divine wrath upon Israel, but would exalt itself and make itself the end instead of the means.

Gill keeps the received word for the nation, every one a hypocrite who served the Lord outwardly only; he spells out that the Assyrian never imagined he was the rod of another's anger but thought himself his own master, and meant not to chastise the Jews but to destroy them and many nations; he offers two readings of the boast about the princes, kings conquered and now ruled or nobles whose wealth made them equal to kings; and he cites a rabbi that what precedes was said before Samaria fell and this after. Calvin makes the charge structural, since uprightness is the chief of the virtues and hypocrisy the mother of all the vices, and the Lord's rod, like a father's, has a fixed destination. He turns the next verse pastorally: when wicked men vomit out their rage they disturb weak minds, as though God could not restrain them, so the prophet steps forward beforehand. On the list of cities he thinks they are fortified places rather than countries and hears the way wicked men talk proudly of what they have done so as to imagine nothing can stand in their way; blinded by pride the Assyrian acknowledges no authority above his own, though none of us can move a finger without God's permission; and at the last he insults not men only but God, and even the gods he himself worshipped.

Wesley adds why the point about the Assyrian's intention stands where it does, that it justifies the judgments afterwards threatened against him, who designed not God's will but the enlarging of his empire. He reduces the boast about the cities to a taunt, that the speaker conquered one place as well as another, the stronger as well as the weaker, and reaches Ellicott's conclusion about the word for idols from the other side, that the speaker uses it of the gods of the nations, Jerusalem's not excepted, by way of contempt, judging them far inferior to the sun, the god of the Assyrians.

debates.question: Is the sending a single act or a standing rule?

positions.view: A standing rule: the verb is best rendered I am wont to send, making it a law of the divine government.
A particular commission against a particular people.

debates.question: Whose words are the boasts, and how far can they be trusted as the Assyrian's own?

positions.view: Substantially his: they match the royal inscriptions exactly, though the word for idols is one the prophet supplied.
His in intention: he thought himself his own master and meant destruction, not chastisement.
His, and blasphemous beyond what he knew, since he insults even the gods he worships.

outliers.note: Reduces the whole section to a single formula, that the instrument would make itself the end instead of the means.

themes: I will send him against an hypocritical nation, and against the people of my wrath will I give him a charge, to take the spoil, and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets.
Howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy and cut off nations not a few.
For he saith, Are not my princes altogether kings?
Is not Calno as Carchemish? is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus?
As my hand hath found the kingdoms of the idols, and whose graven images did excel them of Jerusalem and of Samaria;
Shall I not, as I have done unto Samaria and her idols, so do to Jerusalem and her idols?

12.pericope_label: Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion... Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith?

schools.summary: Ellicott would read the opening word as a simple and rather than a wherefore, the proud king's speech being interrupted by the reassertion that he is only an instrument and will himself be punished when his work is done; he takes the fruit of the stout heart to include all the words and acts in which the arrogance had shown itself, calls the boasting another reproduction of the royal inscriptions' style, and identifies the practice behind one clause, merging independent nations into one empire being pursued more systematically by Assyria than by other conquerors, whose kings exulted in the title of remover of boundaries and landmarks. On the nest he finds an almost verbal parallel in an Assyrian inscription and a king who is a colossal fowler in others, and hears in the closing figure what later Christian writers meant in calling a barbarian conqueror the scourge of God. Delitzsch supplies the mechanism of the turn: when God had punished to the point where he could go no further without destroying Israel, contrary to his mercy and truth, the punishing would turn against the instrument, which falls under the curse of all ungodly selfishness.

Gill turns the boasting inward, that if such arrogance in civil things is resented by God, much more in religious, when men ascribe salvation to their free will and the works of their hands; and he marks where the king's speech ends and the prophet's begins, deriding a boast as absurd as an axe ascribing the felling to itself. Calvin finds two clauses in the twelfth verse, that God will punish a wicked king and that the time is not yet come, and observes that wicked men act as though God were not in heaven; he reads the strength boasted of as vast armies collected out of many nations and says the prudence claimed is bestowed on tricks and dishonest cunning; and on the axe he says the case is exactly that of a tool despising the hand that sets it in motion and priding itself on an activity it has no power of its own to produce.

Clarke would translate the fruit as the effect, following the Chaldee, which renders the word works; he works on the odd phrase that closes the passage, rendering it its master, and explains the idiom behind it, a Hebrew way of joining the negative particle to a noun to express total absence of the thing named, as in help to the no-strength, the arm of the no-power, counsel to the no-wisdom. Wesley reads the whole work as the chastising of God's people for as long as he sees fit, and calls the claim to have gathered all the riches of the earth a hyperbole not unusual in such mouths, noting how birds hover and mourn over a robbed nest.

debates.question: What is the fruit of the stout heart?

positions.view: All the words and acts in which the king's arrogance had shown itself.
The effect, or works, following the Chaldee rather than the received word.

debates.question: When does the punishment turn on the instrument?

positions.view: At the point where further punishing would destroy Israel, which God's mercy and truth forbid.
At a time God has fixed but which is not yet come.

outliers.note: Explains the chapter's oddest phrase by a Hebrew idiom of negation, citing parallels for the no-strength, the no-power and the no-wisdom.
Finds the comfort of the passage in the scourge-of-God idea, that a conqueror's lust for power may be limitless but God's compassion sets the limit.

themes: Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks.

For he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I am prudent: and I have removed the bounds of the people, and have robbed their treasures, and I have put down the inhabitants like a valiant man:

And my hand hath found as a nest the riches of the people: and as one gathereth eggs that are left, have I gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped.

Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it? as if the rod should shake itself against them that lift it up, or as if the staff should lift up itself, as if it were no wood.

16.pericope_label: Therefore shall the Lord, the Lord of hosts, send among his fat ones leanness... And the rest of the trees of his forest shall be few, that a child may write them

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the fat ones the army's warriors, says the fire burning the king's glory is explained next as the wrath of God, divides the thorns from the glory of the forest as the host from the captains, and finds the emphatic in one day pointing to a single catastrophe such as the one that afterwards destroyed that army; on the difficult last clause of the eighteenth verse he reports that our version gives the extremity of exhaustion, the standard-bearer being chosen for strength and stature, but judges the truer rendering to be that a sick man pines away, and observes that numbering a host was the royal scribe's work, often so shown in the Assyrian sculptures, the survivors here being so few that a boy who could count only on his fingers would be skilled enough. Delitzsch counts three epithets designating God by his all-controlling omnipotence, one of which this prophet always uses of judicial manifestations; he makes fire and light one thing in God, the former resolved in his self-life into the latter, so the word for holy stands parallel to that for light; he reads the pair of nouns as a human forest and park, forest because the army came from many nations, garden ground because it boasted the beauty of men and armour; and he renders the disputed clause as when a sick man dies.

Gill says the titles humble the boaster, Lord of greater armies than the Assyrian commanded, has the Lord who calls his own out of darkness stand as a consuming fire to everyone else, allows the glory of the forest to mean the chief officers or the plunder taken from Egypt, and reports the rabbinic tradition that no more than ten escaped with their king, with a stricter version putting it at five, named. Calvin reads the fatness and the fire as the wealth and forces the king trusted in, defending the first because prosperity is commonly likened to fatness and horses grown too fat become refractory; he puts the light and fire as physics, two things in one flame producing contrary effects; he denies that the second noun of the eighteenth verse is a proper name, taking it for an appellative meaning rich soil since the mountain of that name could not be said to belong to Assyria; and he makes the point about the survivors from the other end, that children can barely count beyond three or four.

Clarke says the glory under which the fire is kindled means all the king could boast of as strong in his forces, and takes the briers and thorns for the common people and the glory of the forest for the nobles, the fire destroying both, so the few who escape look like brands plucked from the burning. Wesley has the king stripped of wealth and might, his army destroyed as fire destroys combustible things cast into it, and keeps the received sense of the last clause, a fallen standard-bearer striking panic into a whole army.

debates.question: What does the clause about the standard-bearer mean?

positions.view: As a sick man pines away; the received rendering of exhaustion is less correct.
As when a sick man dies.
The received sense: a fallen standard-bearer strikes panic into a whole army.
Ten by rabbinic tradition, or five on a stricter version that names them.
So few that a boy counting on his fingers could number them.
So few that children, who can barely count beyond three or four, could tell them.

outliers.note: Denies that the second noun of the eighteenth verse is the place-name it looks like, on the ground that the mountain in question could not be said to belong to Assyria.

themes: Therefore shall the Lord, the Lord of hosts, send among his fat ones leanness; and under his glory he shall kindle a burning like the burning of a fire.
And the light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame: and it shall burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day;
And shall consume the glory of his forest, and of his fruitful field, both soul and body: and they shall be as when a standardbearer fainteth.
And the rest of the trees of his forest shall be few, that a child may write them.

20.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the remnant of Israel... shall stay upon the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth... For the Lord GOD of hosts shall make a consumption, even determined, in the midst of all the land

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that for Assyria's remnant there is as yet no word of hope, identifies the smiter Israel will lean on no longer as the Assyrian king whose protection an earlier king had courted instead of trusting the Holy One of Israel, and finds the Immanuel promise behind the form of the words about the returning remnant, the title of the mighty God reminding men of the Child who was to bear it. He also insists that the word remnant has an aspect of severity as well as promise, the restoration being for the remnant only, and renders the closing clause a finished and decisive work overflowing with righteousness, punitive and corrective at once. Delitzsch presses the identification further: the title is God as historically manifested in the heir of David, and where another prophet sets the Lord and the second David side by side, this one sees them as one, so in New Testament language it would be to God in Christ; he also reads the passage as consolation, since in these more inward addresses the prophet means not to threaten but to comfort.

Gill hears the allusion to the prophet's son's name as a pledge of deliverance and allows a return from captivity, a return to God by repentance, or, as he prefers, a turning to Christ; on the consumption he denies it means the destruction of Judea and makes it the accomplishing of an absolute decree concerning the remnant's salvation, the decree of election, standing not upon works but upon God's sovereign will. Calvin offers the same lesson as consolation, that because it is painful to endure calamities the Lord shows us their result, so we may consider their design and bear them more patiently, the chastisement being as necessary as medicine; and he strikes at those who reckoned it enough to be Abraham's descendants after the flesh before comforting the godly, so the shrinking of their number should not take them unawares.

Clarke says flatly that the mighty God is the Messiah, named in the preceding chapter. On the closing clause he observes that neither the Greek version, nor the apostle who follows it closely, nor any ancient version notices the word rendered overflowing, which seems to him to give an idea not easily reconciled with the words it stands among, and passes on a conjecture that its last two letters have been transposed and the true reading is judging, with strict justice. Wesley confines the promise to such Jews as were preserved from the Assyrian scourge, and takes the destruction as decreed by God's fixed counsel and certain to be executed, overflowing them like a deluge, with justice and yet clemency, since a remnant was spared where all might have perished.

Henry recalls that the Lord was to perform his whole work upon Zion and finds here what it is: the conversion of some, to whom the providence is sanctified and yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness though for the present grievous, and these only a remnant beside a people once as the sea sand.

debates.question: Whom does the remnant return to?

positions.view: The Messiah, the same person named in the preceding chapter.
God as manifested in the heir of David, the two seen as one; in New Testament language, God in Christ.
The bearer of the Immanuel promise, whom the title would have called to mind.
The Lord, whether by return from captivity, by repentance, or by faith in Christ.

debates.question: What does the overflowing of the closing clause mean?

positions.view: Nothing: the word is probably corrupt, since no ancient version notices it, and should read judging, with strict justice.
A finished and decisive work overflowing with righteousness, punitive and corrective at once.
A decreed destruction overflowing them like a deluge, with justice and yet clemency.
The accomplishing of the decree of election, which secures the remnant's salvation.

outliers.note: Doubts a word of the received text on the ground that neither the Greek version nor the apostle quoting it takes any notice of it, and proposes a transposition of letters instead.

themes: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the remnant of Israel, and such as are escaped of the house of Jacob, shall no more again stay upon him that smote them; but shall stay upon the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.
The remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God.
For though thy people Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet a remnant of them shall return: the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness.
For the Lord God of hosts shall make a consumption, even determined, in the midst of all the land.

24.pericope_label: Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD of hosts, O my people that dwellest in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian... his burden shall be taken away from off thy shoulder, and his yoke from off thy neck

schools.summary: Ellicott draws the practical conclusion, that the people should not give way to panic as in an earlier reign but abide the Assyrian march with the tranquillity of faith, and finds the ground of hope inside the phrase about Egypt itself, since Pharaoh's cruelty was followed by the exodus; he quotes the Jewish proverb that when the tale of bricks is doubled deliverance is near, takes the indignation for the wrath poured out on God's people which ceases so that God's anger may turn to their enemies' destruction, observes that in the old history the names of the Midianite chiefs are also the names of the places where they fell, and makes the repeated Egyptian formula the turning point, an evil omen a few verses earlier returning as an augury of good. On the last verse he calls the received English scarcely intelligible, though it suggests that the anointing marked out Judah's kings and priests as a consecrated people, and reports that most commentators render it by reason of the fat, the figure being a bullock grown too fat for the yoke to go round his neck. Delitzsch cautions that the expression rendered a very little while does not date from the actual present.

Gill makes the little while a few days, the Assyrian army being destroyed by an angel shortly after it came against Jerusalem, and keeps to the historical burden of the last verse, the tribute imposed on Hezekiah. Calvin explains why the comfort is addressed to some and not all, since many gloried in God's name while few performed what they professed, and after the kingdom's fall the godly might have judged their own case by the case of others; he extends the horizon of the promise much further than the siege, to the overthrow of the city, the razing of the temple and the carrying away of the inhabitants, saying that commentators who neglect this cannot make the statements agree; he notes that the prophet says scourge rather than rod, meaning the Lord will treat the enemies more harshly than they treated the Jews; and he declines to fix the deliverance to one event, partly agreeing with those who take it of the overthrow of the besieging army but extending the prediction further.

Clarke thinks the ambiguity of the phrase about Egypt designed: the Assyrian lifts his rod on the march up from Egypt, threatening God's people as Pharaoh had when he pursued them to the sea, but God in his turn will lift his rod over the sea as he did then, and the imitator of the Egyptians meets their end. On the last verse he follows a bishop who abandons the difficult clause altogether, adopting the Greek reading from your shoulders because no good sense could be made of the present text, and adds an archbishop's conjecture, equally at a loss, of reading sons of oil, understood of the Jews as God's anointed. Wesley reads the Egyptian phrase plainly, as the Egyptians formerly did, takes the indignation as ceasing when vengeance is fully executed, and keeps the anointing, referring it to David, for whose sake God gave deliverances to later ages, and principally to the Messiah, of whom David was a type.

Henry notes that the prophet distinguishes the precious from the vile because providence does, speaking terror in the invasion to the hypocrites who were the people of God's wrath and comfort to the sincere who were the people of his love: the judgment came for the first, the deliverance for the second.

debates.question: How long is the very little while?

positions.view: A few days, until the angel destroyed the besieging army.
Not measured from the actual present at all.
Long enough to cover the later calamities too, the city's overthrow and the captivity.

debates.question: What is the anointing that destroys the yoke?

positions.view: Perhaps the consecration of Judah's kings and priests, though most render the word by reason of the fat, a bullock too fat for its yoke.
Nothing recoverable: the clause should be abandoned for the Greek reading from your shoulders.
David, and principally the Messiah of whom David was a type.

outliers.note: Finds the ground of hope inside the very phrase that sounds most threatening, since the Egyptian oppression was followed by the exodus, and quotes the proverb that when the tale of bricks is doubled deliverance is near.

themes: Therefore thus saith the Lord God of hosts, O my people that dwellest in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrian: he shall smite thee with a rod, and shall lift up his staff against thee, after the manner of Egypt.
For yet a very little while, and the indignation shall cease, and mine anger in their destruction.
And the Lord of hosts shall stir up a scourge for him according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb: and as his rod was upon the sea, so shall he lift it up after the manner of Egypt.
And it shall come to pass in that day, that his burden shall be taken away from off thy shoulder, and his yoke from off thy neck, and the yoke shall be destroyed because of the anointing.

28.pericope_label: He is come to Aiath, he is passed to Migron; at Michmash he hath laid up his carriages... And he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one

schools.summary: Delitzsch calls the description of the march, aesthetically considered, one of the most magnificent human poetry has produced. Ellicott marks a clean break here, the new section joined to what precedes only by subject, and cites an inscription in which the Assyrian calls himself subduer of the lands of Judah as putting the invasion beyond doubt; on the closing verses he hears another pressure of the strong hand of God, the prophet telling the invader he shall come so far and no farther, and notes that the boughs and thickets repeat the earlier imagery, with the edge that Assyrian kings boasted of cutting down the forests of the nations they conquered.

Gill notes that the word for the cry serves also for a joyful sound and for the neighing of horses, has one town's inhabitants removing on the news, has the invader stop short and stay briefly to prepare his army for the next day's march, reports the Jewish tradition that he performed all his journeys in one day, takes the bough for the king and his army cut off in terrible manner, the word meaning a tree's ornament and glory, and makes the iron of the last verse an angel excelling in strength. Calvin explains why the itinerary is given at all, that it sets the march before their eyes so the godly may stand firm, showing that the Assyrians did not move a step but by God's appointment; he doubts the view that the Jordan is meant by the passage and draws the inference the others leave unstated, that the enemy passing unopposed shows all thought of a stand in open country was given up; he takes the cry for howling heard at a distance and notes that Hebrew calls cities daughters; he reads the shaking of one town as exaggerated speech for a people's disorderly flight; and he prefers the reading that makes the invader halt with much of the day still before him to prepare the siege.

Clarke says the terror spreading through the places as the army advances is expressed with great brevity but finely diversified, and fixes the ground, all near Jerusalem, from the first town northward to the last westward; he identifies the strait of Michmash as the passage crossed, a narrow way between two hills where a great army might have been opposed by a far smaller one; he follows the Syriac in rendering one clause hearken unto her and answer her, holding that the prophet plays on a place-name that may have come from an echo, and quotes a lexicon giving it the sense of responses; he reports that many manuscripts, four editions and three versions read bough as wine-press; and on the closing clause he holds with two commentators that the mighty one is the angel who smote the army and that the Assyrian king is the one overthrown. Wesley describes the invasion as present, the baggage left so the march may be faster, has the people flee to Jerusalem for fear, puts the mother city and her lesser towns, and makes the bough the top bough and names the king.

debates.question: Which passage does the army cross?

positions.view: The strait of Michmash, a narrow way defensible by a far smaller force.
The same strait, not the Jordan; and the enemy passing it unopposed shows the open country had been abandoned.

debates.question: What is the mighty one by whom Lebanon falls?

positions.view: The angel who smote the army; the alternative rendering makes the high cedars fall instead.
An angel excelling in strength, figured as iron.
God himself, saying to the invader that he shall come so far and no farther.

outliers.note: Praises the itinerary purely as writing, calling it one of the most magnificent descriptions human poetry has produced.
Builds an argument on the possibility that a place-name in the list was itself derived from a remarkable echo, and renders the clause accordingly.

themes: He is come to Aiath, he is passed to Migron; at Michmash he hath laid up his carriages:
They are gone over the passage: they have taken up their lodging at Geba; Ramah is afraid; Gibeah of Saul is fled.
Lift up thy voice, O daughter of Gallim: cause it to be heard unto Laish, O poor Anathoth.
Madmenah is removed; the inhabitants of Gebim gather themselves to flee.
As yet shall he remain at Nob that day: he shall shake his hand against the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.
Behold, the Lord, the Lord of hosts, shall lop the bough with terror: and the high ones of stature shall be hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled.
And he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one.
